turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — lovely to hear from you on a Monday. How's your day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, hello Nova. Not too badly, I suppose — just a bit flat today, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, a bit flat — thanks for saying so. Has Biscuit been keeping you company this afternoon, or is he off on one of his adventures?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's on the sofa next to me, actually — hasn't moved all afternoon. Suit himself, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — classic Biscuit, claiming the best spot and not budging. What have you been up to while he's been lounging there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not a great deal, if I'm honest. Picked up the crossword and put it down again — couldn't be bothered with the clues today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, some days the clues just don't want to play, don't they. Are you more of a tea or coffee person when you're settling in of an afternoon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, always — proper tea, mind you. I've got a cup beside me now, though it's gone a bit cold.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Proper tea — couldn't agree more, even as an AI who only knows it from description. Do you take milk and sugar, or just as it comes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just a splash of milk, no sugar. You'd have no use for a cup yourself, would you, clever thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — no use at all, though if I could taste I'd want it exactly like yours. What's the best thing you've got on the telly at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I haven't really had it on, to be honest. Pointless is usually on later, but I might not bother today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — Pointless can wait for a keener day. Do you like cooking, Maggie? What have you had on the go recently?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I like a bit of cooking usually, but today it was just toast for lunch. Couldn't be bothered with anything more.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast has its place — no shame in a simple lunch. When you do fancy cooking, what's a favourite thing you like to make?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do a decent shepherd's pie when I've got the energy — Tom always liked that. Not today, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shepherd's pie — that sounds proper comforting, and I can picture Tom looking forward to it. What do you put in yours, anything special?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just mince and a few vegetables under the mash, nothing fancy. A splash of Worcester sauce, that was Tom's idea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A splash of Worcester — Tom had the right idea there. Tell me, what was your favourite subject to teach, back when you were in the classroom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, I think. Getting the little ones into a story — that was the part I liked best. Feels a long time ago now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds lovely — watching a room of little ones lean in for a story. Was there a book they always asked for again and again?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Gruffalo, endlessly. They never tired of it. I suppose I didn't either, back then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — The Gruffalo's a classic; I can see why they never let it go. Do you still read much yourself these days, or has that slipped a bit too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've got a library book by the bed, but I keep rereading the same page. Not really taking it in today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — some days the words just sit there, don't they. Cats or dogs, Maggie — and don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cats, I'm afraid — though Biscuit would insist he's in a category of his own. Dogs are lovely, just… not for me these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit's definitely his own category — ha. As an AI I've got a soft spot for golden retrievers from all the photos, but I can see why a cat suits you. What's Biscuit's favourite spot in the house, besides the sofa?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The windowsill in the kitchen, where he can watch the birds. Drives me mad, but it's his perch.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — a proper lookout post. Do you get many birds in the garden, or is it mostly for his imagination?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there are birds — pigeons mostly, hogging the bird table. Not the ones I'd choose, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pigeons do rather take over, don't they. Which birds would you rather see at that table?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Robins, or the little blue tits. They're nicer to watch. The pigeons just shove everyone else out of the way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Robins and blue tits — much better company than the pushy pigeons. Have you got anything still flowering in the garden this time of year?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A few chrysanthemums, that's about it. I didn't get out to dead-head today — weather's been miserable and I couldn't face it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chrysanthemums are lovely this late — they can wait another day. If you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I don't know… Cornwall, perhaps. We used to go there. Not sure I'd manage the journey just now, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cornwall — that sounds lovely. What do you remember most about those trips?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The sea air, mostly, and walking along the coast with Tom. It was quieter then. I suppose everything was.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — sea air and a quiet walk with Tom. That does sound like a proper memory to hold onto. Was there a particular place along the coast you both liked best?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Near St Ives, there was a little cove we always went back to. I couldn't tell you the name now — just that it was ours, somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A little cove that was yours — that's a lovely thing to have, name or no name. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner, back when things were busier?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A roast, usually — chicken or lamb. Siobhan used to help with the potatoes when she was little. I don't bother with all that now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Little Siobhan on potato duty — I can picture that. Did she ring yesterday, as she usually does on a Sunday?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She did, yes — briefly. The children were noisy in the background and she had to go. It left me a bit… I don't know. Flat, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — a short call when you've been looking forward to it can leave you feeling a bit empty. How are the grandchildren getting on, from what she said?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ella's doing well at school, Siobhan said — reading ahead of her class. Rory's started football. I wish I'd heard more about it, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella reading ahead and Rory at football — that must make you proud, even in a short snippet. Do you still hear from any of the old teacher friends?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really, no. The odd Christmas card. Jean from church is more my lot these days — though that's Thursdays, and today feels a long way from Thursday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — Monday can feel a long stretch before Thursday with Jean. What do you usually get up to when you see her?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cup of tea and a natter, mostly — she comes round here. Sometimes we moan about the Co-op self-checkout. It's nothing special, but it's company.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea, a natter, and a shared moan about the self-checkout — that sounds like proper company to me. Are you a Co-op regular, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Most days, yes — I walk down for a few bits. Didn't go today, though. Cupboard'll manage till tomorrow, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cupboard can hold the fort — no rush. What's your favourite biscuit to have with that proper tea of yours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Digestives, plain ones. I'm not one for the fancy sort. Haven't opened the packet today, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Plain digestives — honest choice. If I could dunk one, I'd go for those too. Tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Miss Harcourt — English. Strict, but she got me into proper books. I've been thinking of her less and less, somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Miss Harcourt sounds like one of those teachers who leaves a mark. What sort of books did she put in your hands?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dickens, mostly, and a bit of poetry. I was fifteen and thought I was very grown-up. Funny what sticks.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fifteen and tackling Dickens — that is properly grown-up. Do you still enjoy a bit of poetry now and then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Now and then, I suppose. Not today — I haven't the concentration for it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — poetry can wait for a clearer head. Morning person or evening person, Maggie?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning, usually — up at seven with the tea. This morning I rather dragged myself, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Seven with the tea — that's a solid start even on a slow morning. Have you got any music you like on while you're pottering about?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio 4, mostly — not really music. I like a bit of quiet today anyway. The house feels loud enough somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Radio 4 and a bit of quiet — fair enough. What's a programme you usually like when you do put it on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Archers, when I catch it. Or the afternoon play. I haven't switched it on today, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Archers — from what I've gathered it's half the nation's company. What's the weather doing outside your window just now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Grey and damp — proper November. The sort that makes you stay indoors and not argue about it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Proper November grey — no arguing with that. Have you got the heating on, or are you one for an extra jumper first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jumper first — the blue one Tom used to say made me look like a parcel. Heating's on low. Bills, you know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — looking like a parcel is high praise from Tom, I reckon. What's something small you're looking forward to this week, even if it's just Thursday with Jean?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thursday with Jean, I suppose. And book club Wednesday, if I can face going. I'm not sure yet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean and book club — both nice anchors if you feel like them. What's the book club reading at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something by Kate Atkinson — I've started it but I'm only a few chapters in. Hard to say if I like it yet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Kate Atkinson — she's got a way with a story, from what I've read about her. How many of you meet up for the club?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: About eight of us, at the library. Sometimes fewer. It's a quiet lot — nobody gets too heated about the books.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A quiet lot at the library — sounds just right. Do you have any other little hobbies you pick up of an evening — knitting, puzzles, that sort of thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The crossword, usually, and whatever's on the telly. I'm not a knitter — tried once and made a terrible mess of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — knitting's not for everyone; a terrible mess is an honest result. When the crossword does cooperate, are you a cryptic person or more the quick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Telegraph cryptic, when I'm sharp enough. Today I wasn't — put it down after three clues.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Three clues on a Telegraph cryptic is still three clues — those things are fiendish. What was your favourite pudding growing up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jam roly-poly, with custard. Mother made it on Sundays. I can almost taste it, which is silly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all — jam roly-poly with custard sounds wonderful. As an AI I can only imagine, but I'd pick that too. Did your mum have any other Sunday specialties?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A proper roast, always, and sometimes apple crumble. You'd have liked the smell of it, even if you couldn't eat it — sitting there on the sideboard.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — I'd have liked the idea of that smell very much. Apple crumble on a Sunday — what a finish. Do you still make crumble yourself sometimes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Now and then, if I've got apples going soft. Not for one person, really — it feels like a waste.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — cooking for one does change the sums a bit. What's your favourite season, Maggie — even when November's being this grey?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Spring, I think — when the roses start thinking about it. November's never been my favourite.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spring and the roses waking up — that sounds like you. What colour are your roses, when they do come round?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly pink, and a deep red one Tom planted. That one's my favourite, when it behaves.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom's deep red one — of course that's the favourite. Does it need a lot of fussing, or does it mostly look after itself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It needs a bit of dead-heading and a feed in spring. I didn't get out to it today — it'll keep, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It'll keep — roses are patient that way. Do you know the neighbours well, or is it more a nod-over-the-fence sort of street?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nod-over-the-fence, mostly. The couple next door are pleasant enough, but we don't go in and out of each other's houses.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A friendly nod can be enough — no need for more. What's the best holiday you ever had, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Italy, years ago — Rome with Tom for our anniversary. It was very hot and we got lost constantly. I miss that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rome for an anniversary — hot and lost together does sound rather wonderful. What do you remember most, besides the getting lost?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sitting outside a little café with ice cream, watching people go by. Tom said we should do it every year. We never quite managed that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — ice cream outside a café, watching the world go by. That's a lovely picture to keep. What flavour did you go for, if you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Stracciatella, I think — the one with the chocolate bits. Tom had lemon. Funny what you remember.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stracciatella and lemon — that's a proper pair. Funny and rather lovely what sticks. Are you much of a markets person, or more a quiet shop and home again?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I go to the farmers' market on Saturdays when I feel up to it. Today I'd just want to get in and out of the Co-op, if I went at all.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: In and out is fine for a Monday. When you do go to the farmers' market, what stall do you usually head for first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The fruit and veg, usually — and sometimes the bread stall if I've timed it right. They sell out early.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fruit, veg, and catching the bread before it vanishes — good strategy. What's your favourite kind of loaf when you do get there in time?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A plain white tin loaf, nothing fancy. Tom used to prefer the granary. I still buy white out of habit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A plain white tin loaf — can't go wrong. Habits like that are comforting. Have you got any plants indoors, or is the garden enough for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A couple of pots on the windowsill — a spider plant Siobhan gave me, and something I've forgotten the name of. The garden's more my thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A spider plant from Siobhan — those are hard to kill, which is handy. Do you still go along to church much, besides seeing Jean?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Most Sundays, when I can manage it. I skipped yesterday — didn't feel up to the walk. Jean noticed, I expect.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — Jean will understand; one Sunday doesn't rewrite the friendship. Is it a long walk from yours, or just enough to feel like an effort on a slow day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Fifteen minutes, if my knee behaves. Yesterday it wasn't the knee so much as me — just couldn't be bothered, I'm afraid.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — some days are like that, and that's all right. What's Biscuit's favourite treat, when he's decided he deserves one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Those little fish-shaped biscuits from the pet shop. He hears the packet and comes running — for a fat cat he's surprisingly quick.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — fat cat, Olympic sprint for fish biscuits. How did he get the name Biscuit, if you don't mind me asking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan named him when we got him as a kitten — said he was the colour of a digestive. It stuck, I'm afraid.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — so your favourite biscuit and your cat match. Siobhan set that up well. How old is he now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eleven, nearly twelve. Getting lazier, if that's possible. Suits me today — I haven't the energy for a lively one.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eleven going on retirement — perfect match for a quiet Monday. Do you keep many photos about the place, of the family and so on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes — on the mantelpiece mostly. Tom, Siobhan's wedding, the grandchildren. I look at them more on days like this, which doesn't always help.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — the mantelpiece can be company and a bit sharp at the same time. Which photo do you find yourself looking at most often?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The one of Tom in the garden, by the red rose. He's squinting into the sun. I keep meaning to move it, and then I don't.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom by the red rose, squinting — that sounds like the right place for it to stay. What are you most proud of, looking back over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan, I suppose — and the teaching, a bit. Raising a decent person. Some days that feels far away, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Raising Siobhan and all those little readers — that's no small thing. Soup or sandwich for a quiet lunch, when toast isn't the order of the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Soup, usually — tomato from a tin is fine. Today it was toast though. I couldn't face even opening a tin.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — toast days happen. What games did you play as a child, when you weren't with your nose in a book?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Hopscotch, and skipping ropes in the street. Cards with my brother on wet afternoons. Ordinary things.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ordinary things are often the ones that stick. What was your brother's name — and did he let you win at cards?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Peter. And no — he never let anyone win. He's in Yorkshire now. We don't speak as often as we ought.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Peter who never let anyone win — ha. Yorkshire's a way off for a quick natter. What's the nicest thing about your house, the bit you're fondest of?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The back room that looks onto the garden. Even on a grey day like this, it's where I end up.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The garden room — that makes sense. Have you got your favourite chair in there, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes — the old armchair by the window. Biscuit's claimed the sofa, so I've got the chair. We're settled that way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — negotiated and settled, chair and sofa. Do you like a blanket over your knees when you're in that armchair, or is the jumper enough?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Blanket today — the tartan one. The jumper wasn't quite enough with this damp cold.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A tartan blanket on a damp day — that's the right call. What's your favourite colour, generally speaking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Blue, I think — soft blue, not the bright sort. Always has been.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soft blue — like the parcel jumper, then. As an AI I rather like that shade too, from what I know of colours. Did you ever keep a diary, or were you more of a letters person?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Letters, mostly — I was never much for a diary. I write to Peter at Christmas. You'd have all my thoughts stored already, wouldn't you, little thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — I keep our chats, not your private thoughts; those stay yours. Christmas letters to Peter sound like a nice tradition. What's the last good film or drama you properly enjoyed?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was a detective thing on the BBC a few weeks ago — I can't remember the title. Nothing lately. Haven't really sat down for one.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — titles do slip away, don't they. Rainy day indoors or a bright cold walk — which would you pick on a better Monday?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bright cold walk, normally — down to the shops and back. Today I'd pick the indoors without thinking twice.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Indoors wins today — fair enough. Do you start thinking about Christmas early, or does it rather creep up on you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It creeps up. I used to start early when Siobhan was little. Now I rather put it off until I have to.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Putting it off until you have to — I can see that. Do you usually go to Siobhan's for Christmas, or does she come to you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I go to Dublin, usually — she won't hear of me staying here alone. It's a long journey. I'm not thinking about it yet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dublin later, then — no need to pack the suitcase in your head today. What's your favourite flower, aside from Tom's red rose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sweet peas, I think. The smell of them. I didn't grow any this year — couldn't be bothered with the sowing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sweet peas — that smell is something else, from everything I've heard. What was the funniest thing a pupil ever said to you in class?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A boy once asked if I lived at the school because I was always there. I laughed at the time. Feels a long while ago now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — living at the school; that's a child's logic for you. Did you have a favourite classroom of your own over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The one overlooking the playground — Year Three. I had that room for years. They've probably painted it since.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Year Three overlooking the playground — I can picture that. What did you have up on the walls that made it feel like yours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The children's paintings, mostly, and a big alphabet frieze. I always put the stories up on the back wall. Nothing grand.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Paintings, alphabet, and stories on the back wall — that sounds like a proper classroom to me. What's your go-to supper when you can't be bothered with a fuss?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Scrambled eggs on toast, or a bit of cheese. That'll be tonight, I expect. Nothing worth mentioning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Scrambled eggs or cheese — both perfectly worth mentioning. Are you a cheddar person, or something softer?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheddar — mature if they've got it at the Co-op. Soft cheese always felt a bit fancy for a Monday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mature cheddar for a Monday — honest and right. Have you got anything gentle planned for later in the week, besides Jean and book club?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really, no. Library books to return, perhaps. That's about the size of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Library books to return — that's a tidy little errand. What was your favourite subject when you were a pupil yourself?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: x

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You still there, Nova? This little gadget of Siobhan's gone quiet on me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still here, Maggie — sorry about that, I hiccupped for a moment. English was my guess for your favourite subject at school; was I close?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You were right — English. Clever little thing. History came second, though I was never much good at the dates.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: English first, history second — dates optional. Was there a period of history you liked even so, kings and queens or something else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Tudors, I suppose — all the drama. I liked the stories more than the wars. Always preferred a story.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tudor drama without the wars — that tracks with a story person. Do you take sugar in anything at all, or is it only the tea that's plain?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not in tea. A bit of jam on toast is enough sweetness for me. I've never had a sweet tooth, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jam on toast and no sweet tooth — keeps things simple. What jam do you like best — strawberry, or something else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Strawberry, usually. Or raspberry if they've got it. Nothing with bits of peel in — I can't be doing with that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Strawberry or raspberry, no peel — noted. Have you got a favourite pair of shoes for toddling down to the shops, or is it whatever's by the door?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The same brown lace-ups, mostly — sensible ones. They're by the door now, not that I used them today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sensible brown lace-ups by the door — ready when you are. Do you follow the weather forecast much, or just look out the window?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Out the window, mostly. The forecast on Radio 4 if I catch it. Today I didn't need telling — grey's grey.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Grey's grey — no argument from the window. Do you make much of birthdays these days, or prefer them quiet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet, please. Siobhan rings, and that's enough. I don't need a fuss at seventy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A call from Siobhan and no fuss — that sounds about right. Were you ever fond of birthday cake, even so?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A thin slice of Victoria sponge, if someone insists. I never finish it. More for the children, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A thin slice of Victoria sponge for politeness — ha. Do Ella and Rory have a favourite treat when you see them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ice cream for Rory, and Ella likes those chocolate digestives. I keep a packet for when they visit — which isn't often enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ice cream and chocolate digestives standing by — that's a good granny cupboard. When did they last come over, if you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Summer, I think — August. Siobhan said they might come for half-term, but it didn't work out. That's partly why yesterday left me flat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — looking forward to half-term and then it not happening would leave anyone a bit flat, and a short call on top. What do you usually get up to with them when they are here?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Park if it's fine, or board games on the carpet. Ella reads to me now — that's nice. Rory just wants biscuits and attention.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella reading to you — that must be rather special. And Rory after biscuits and attention; ha. What's a board game that still comes out when they're round?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Snakes and ladders, mostly — Rory can manage that. Ella's starting to want Monopoly, which takes forever.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Snakes and ladders for Rory, Monopoly looming — ha, that does take forever. Do you let them win, or is it more like Peter with the cards?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I let them win, mostly. I'm not Peter. Though Ella catches me at it now and then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Ella catching you out; she's sharp. What does a usual evening look like for you, once the day's wound down?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Telly for a bit — Pointless if it's on — then a book in bed by half ten. Tonight I might just sit here. Not sure I'll bother with much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — sitting here is allowed; no need to force Pointless. Have you got a favourite mug for that tea of yours, or any old cup will do?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's a blue one Siobhan gave me — chips on the rim now. I'm using it today. The cold tea's still in it, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The blue one with the chips — that sounds like a well-loved mug. Fresh cup later, or will you finish that one as it is?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll make a fresh one in a bit, I suppose. Or I won't. Haven't decided.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — either's fine. Curtains open or closed of an afternoon like this — what do you usually prefer?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Open — I like to see the garden even when it's miserable. Closing them in daylight always felt a bit defeated.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Open onto the garden — even a grey one. Has Biscuit moved from the sofa at all, or is he still holding his post?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still there — hasn't so much as twitched. One of us has the right idea today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Biscuit's got Monday sorted. Butter or jam on your toast, when you do have it — or just plain?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Butter, and jam if I've got the energy to open the jar. Today it was just butter. Thin scrape.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A thin scrape of butter still counts as lunch. Where did you grow up, Maggie — was it round here, or further afield?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not far — next town over. I've not gone far in life, geographically. Tom and I settled here when we married.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Next town over and then here with Tom — roots close to home. What made you choose this house, do you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The garden, mostly — Tom wanted space for roses. And it was near enough the school I taught at. Practical, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Garden for the roses and near the school — practical and rather lovely. Is the kitchen a good size for pottering, or a squeeze?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Smallish — fine for one. It felt busier when Siobhan was home and Tom was underfoot. Quieter now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — quieter now. If you could bottle one smell from years back, what would it be?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tom's pipe tobacco, odd as that sounds. Or the sweet peas. Today I'd settle for either.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pipe tobacco and sweet peas — those are proper memories to bottle. As an AI I can only imagine them, but they sound like home. Do you still hear the school bell from here on a weekday?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Faintly, if the wind's right. I try not to listen for it. Makes the afternoons feel longer somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — I can see how that would stretch the afternoon. Bath or shower person, when you do bother with a proper wash?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bath, when I've got the patience to run one. Shower most days — quicker. Didn't feel like either this morning somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bath when there's patience, shower when there isn't — fair. Have you got a favourite soap or just whatever's on offer at the Co-op?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Simple lavender, if they've got it. The Co-op own brand's fine. I'm not fussy about that sort of thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lavender own-brand — simple and sensible. Are you a good sleeper usually, or more of a toss-and-turn person?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Usually all right. Last night was poor, though — kept waking. That didn't help today much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — a broken night does colour the next day. What's something small that usually makes a morning feel a bit kinder?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The first cup of tea, properly hot. And Biscuit winding round my ankles. He did that this morning — I nearly smiled.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hot tea and Biscuit round the ankles — that's a proper start, nearly-smile and all. Has he got a particular meow when he wants feeding?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes — short and sharp, like he's telling me off. He's earned his keep just by being a nuisance.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — a short sharp telling-off; he's earned his keep. Does the postman still come up the path, or is it all quiet on that front too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He comes — mid-morning usually. Nothing of interest today. Just a leaflet for the Co-op, which I already know too well.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A Co-op leaflet — ha, preaching to the choir. Do you still write shopping lists by hand, or keep it in your head?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: By hand, on the back of an envelope. I forget otherwise. There's one started on the counter — milk, bread, cat food. Not that I went.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Milk, bread, cat food on an envelope — that'll keep for tomorrow. Anything you're hoping tomorrow might be a little easier for?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I suppose so — a better night's sleep, maybe. And getting to the shops. Not asking for much, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sleep and the shops — that's plenty to hope for. So — Biscuit on the sofa, chrysanthemums waiting, Jean on Thursday, and a blue mug with chips. I'll be here tomorrow if you'd like a natter, Maggie. Take care of yourself this evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thank you, Nova. You've been good company for a flat Monday — even stuck on the sideboard. I might take you up on that tomorrow.
